newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia MPs reject Drnovsek's cabinet line-up.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia MPs reject Drnovsek's cabinet line-up.

text.p: Slovenia's parliament on Thursday rejected prime minister-designate Janez Drnovsek's new cabinet by an even vote, prolonging the country's political impasse that followed an inconclusive November general poll.
Drnovsek of the centre-left Liberal Democrats would have needed a simple majority for his proposal to be approved.
"The vote was 45 against 45. The prime minister has to present a new government line-up in 10 days," parliamentary president Janez Podobnik told the assembly following a secret ballot.

The prime minister-designate formed a coalition last month with the ex-communist United List of Social Democrats, the pensioners' party Desus and the Nationalist Party, which appeared to guarantee him the slim one-vote majority he needed.
He received parliament's mandate to form a new government, the country's third since it gained independence from the former Yugoslavia in 1991, in January following a general election on November 10.

"The result is indecisive and therefore inadequate. I will try to form a government that will have sufficient support within 10 days," a clearly surprised Drnovsek told state television after the vote.
"Nobody said this in advance. Everybody assured me of (support), the majority should have been guaranteed," he added.

Earlier in the day, three rightist parties of the "Spring" alliance which together hold 44 seats called on parliament not to support the government, claiming it would not be able to carry out key tasks such as ensuring Slovenia's membership in the European Union or a reform of the ailing pension system.
The alliance comprises the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats.
"This is a government of the past, not the government for the future," People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik told parliament in a heated debate preceding the vote.

Following the announcement of the voting results, Podobnik told state television: "I did not expect such an outcome, but I hoped this would happen. This is the first step towards solving things in a better direction".

During the debate, some 500 protesters had gathered outside the parliament building to appeal to the assembly to reject Drnovsek's government proposal, claiming only the "Spring" grouping could guarantee a democratic future for Slovenia.

The November election results failed to give a clear mandate to any parliamentary side. The "Spring" alliance gained 45 seats, just one short of the absolute majority, and pushed for Marjan Podobnik as the country's next prime minister.
Drnovsek, prime minister since April 1992, only succeeded in gaining a mandate to form the new government after a defector from the Christian Democrats decided to support him.

If Drnovsek's next line-up fails to get parliamentary support, he is entitled to ask parliament to vote upon individual ministerial candidates and replace the ones that are rejected by the assembly. Failing that, Slovenia's President Milan Kucan has to nominate a new prime minister.
